# Mission

Your team will build a complete analysis from a dataset that you choose, document and explore.

The project is not an exercise where every step is specified in advance. It asks you to formulate a question, justify your choices, produce a reproducible analysis and communicate a useful result to readers who do not already know your work.

# Objectives

At the end of the project, your repository should show that your team can:

- formulate a clear, feasible data-analysis question;
- document a dataset's source, structure and limitations;
- prepare data with readable and reproducible code;
- produce visualizations and results that answer the question;
- interpret results carefully;
- communicate the project in a short presentation and a final summary;
- collaborate transparently in a GitHub repository.

# Dataset

Choose a manageable dataset for a first complete analysis.

The dataset should normally meet the following criteria:

- at least 50 observations;
- between 5 and 25 useful variables;
- at least one numeric variable and one categorical variable;
- a format that can be read in R, such as CSV, XLSX, RDS, JSON or data obtained from an API;
- an identifiable and citable source.

Datasets used directly in course modules, challenges or exercises should not be reused as the main project dataset, unless explicitly approved. You may reuse the same technical skills.

Possible sources:

- [Donnees Quebec](https://www.donneesquebec.ca/)
- [Government of Canada Open Data Portal](https://open.canada.ca/en/open-data)
- [Statistics Canada](https://www.statcan.gc.ca/)
- [TidyTuesday](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday)
- [Google Dataset Search](https://datasetsearch.research.google.com/)
- [Harvard Dataverse](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/)

Before confirming your choice, check that:

- the file or API can be imported in R with course tools;
- the license or terms of use allow course work;
- the variables can answer a precise question;
- the dataset does not contain unnecessary sensitive or identifying information;
- the source can be cited clearly in the report and presentation.

# GitHub repository

The project starts from the `STT-1100/projet` template repository. Your team repository should remain clean throughout the session.

Expected structure:

```text
.
|-- README.md
|-- CONSIGNES.md
|-- data/
|   |-- README.md
|   |-- raw/
|   `-- processed/
|-- scripts/
|   |-- 00_setup.R
|   |-- 01_import_clean.R
|   `-- 02_analysis.R
|-- proposition/
|   `-- proposition.qmd
|-- presentation/
|   |-- presentation.qmd
|   `-- style.css
|-- figures/
`-- outputs/
```

The `README.md` file is the final project summary. The `CONSIGNES.md` file is an internal guide for using the template and checking deliverables.

Your repository should also follow a few practical rules:

- an external reader should understand the project without oral explanation;
- scripts should run in a reasonable order;
- generated files should remain separate from raw data;
- data that cannot be shared should be replaced by clear documentation;
- temporary files, duplicates and abandoned trials should be removed.

# Workflow

## 1. Proposal

The proposal stabilizes your question, data and work plan. Submit `proposition/proposition.qmd` according to the official schedule posted on Brio.

The proposal must contain:

1. an introduction presenting the context, objective and main question;
2. a description of the data, including source, observational unit, important variables and known limitations;
3. an analysis plan explaining planned transformations, first graphs, comparisons or models, and feasibility risks.

Recommended length: 2 to 4 rendered pages, excluding appendices and exploratory graphs.

### Proposal grading

| Criterion | Points |
|---|---:|
| Clear, relevant and feasible question | 5 |
| Description and provenance of the data | 5 |
| Coherent and realistic analysis plan | 5 |
| Total | 15 |

## 2. Development

After the proposal, your team builds the analysis in the repository.

Development should leave readable traces:

- organized scripts in `scripts/`;
- raw data kept in `data/raw/` when sharing is permitted by the license;
- cleaned or intermediate data in `data/processed/`;
- data dictionary in `data/README.md`;
- exported figures in `figures/` when relevant;
- intermediate results in `outputs/` when relevant.

If the data cannot be shared publicly, clearly explain how to obtain them or how to reproduce the analysis within the permitted limits.

## 3. Presentation

The presentation lasts 15 minutes maximum. Every member must speak.

Use the `presentation/presentation.qmd` file provided in the template. It produces HTML slides with Quarto and supports a presentation style close to `xaringan`, while keeping a `.qmd` workflow.

The presentation must cover:

- the question and why it matters;
- the source and limitations of the data;
- important preparation or cleaning choices;
- the main results;
- at least one central visualization;
- the limits of the analysis;
- a careful conclusion or recommendation.

### Presentation grading

| Criterion | Points |
|---|---:|
| Time management and oral clarity | 6 |
| Question, context and relevance of the data | 7 |
| Quality of the analysis and methodological choices | 12 |
| Visual quality of slides and graphs | 10 |
| Interpretation, limitations and critical thinking | 10 |
| Total | 45 |

## 4. Final summary

The final summary is the root `README.md` file. It should allow an external reader to quickly understand what your team did.

The final summary must contain:

- the project title and team member names;
- the main question;
- a short description of the data;
- the main analysis steps;
- the most important results;
- one central figure or table, if relevant;
- limitations;
- references and dataset citation;
- a link to the rendered HTML presentation.

### Final summary grading

| Criterion | Points |
|---|---:|
| Clear synthesis of question, data and method | 6 |
| Results well explained and tied to the question | 5 |
| Limitations, references and link to the presentation | 4 |
| Total | 15 |

# Reproducibility and organization

Reproducibility is assessed across the whole repository, not only in one file.

| Criterion | Points |
|---|---:|
| Repository structure is compliant and easy to navigate | 5 |
| Code is clear, scripts run and objects are well named | 5 |
| Data are documented, provenance is indicated and unnecessary files are removed | 5 |
| Total | 15 |

# Teamwork

Teamwork is mandatory. Contributions must be visible in GitHub history.

Each team will also complete a peer evaluation according to the format specified on Brio.

| Criterion | Points |
|---|---:|
| Contributions are visible, shared and coherent with the project | 5 |
| Peer evaluation and team accountability | 5 |
| Total | 10 |

# Final evaluation

| Component | Points |
|---|---:|
| Proposal | 15 |
| Presentation | 45 |
| Final summary in `README.md` | 15 |
| Repository reproducibility and organization | 15 |
| Teamwork and peer evaluation | 10 |
| Total | 100 |

# Before the final submission

Before the final submission, your team should be able to answer yes to the following questions:

- The `README.md` tells the project story from beginning to end.
- The HTML presentation is rendered and the link works.
- Important scripts are in `scripts/` and have clear names.
- Data are documented in `data/README.md`.
- Unnecessary files have been removed.
- The main results are explicitly connected to the question.
- Limitations and sources are visible.
- Team contributions are visible in the GitHub history.

# Advice

- Start with a simple question and improve it gradually.
- Test data import before committing too far.
- Commit often with explicit messages.
- Keep generated files, raw data and intermediate results clearly separated.
- Reread your repository as if you were discovering it for the first time.
- Official submission procedures, dates and administrative adjustments are always those posted on Brio.
